content: Carbonyl reductase 1, commonly referred to as CBR1, is an enzyme encoded by the CBR1 gene in humans. This enzyme is a member of the short-chain dehydrogenases/reductases (SDR) family, which are NADPH-dependent oxidoreductases. These enzymes exhibit broad substrate specificity, acting on various carbonyl compounds, including quinones, prostaglandins, and xenobiotics. The CBR1 gene also produces alternatively spliced transcript variants. Carbonyl reductase is a monomeric enzyme that relies on NADPH as a cofactor to reduce carbonyl compounds. It is widely distributed across human tissues. Another gene encoding a related enzyme, CRB3, is located near the CBR1 gene on chromosome 21q. CBR1 is involved in the metabolism of numerous toxic environmental quinones and pharmacologically significant compounds, such as the chemotherapeutic agent doxorubicin. Research has demonstrated that CBR1 plays a protective role in mitigating oxidative stress, neurodegeneration, and apoptosis. Additionally, CBR1 inactivates lipid aldehydes during oxidative stress, suggesting its role in safeguarding cells from oxidative damage. To date, two non-synonymous polymorphisms have been identified in the CBR1 gene. One of these, the CBR1 V88I polymorphism, results in a substitution of valine with isoleucine at position 88 of the amino acid sequence. In vitro studies using recombinant proteins have shown that the CBR1 V88 isoform exhibits a higher maximum velocity (Vmax) when metabolizing substrates such as menadione (vitamin K3) and daunorubicin. Furthermore, studies on human liver cytosols have revealed that a polymorphism in the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of the CBR1 gene (rs9024) is associated with elevated levels of the cardiotoxic metabolite doxorubicinol. The human CBR1 gene is located on chromosome 21 at position q22.13 and consists of eight exons. The enzyme encoded by this gene is composed of 277 amino acids and is expressed in various human tissues, including the liver, epidermis, stomach, small intestine, kidney, neuronal cells, and smooth muscle fibers. CBR1 exhibits high catalytic efficiency with substrates such as quinones, including ubiquinone-1 and tocopherolquinone (vitamin E). Ubiquinones are integral components of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, while tocopherolquinone protects biological membrane lipids from peroxidation. These functions highlight the enzyme's critical role as an oxidation-reduction catalyst in biological processes. CBR1 has been implicated in tumor progression. Reduced expression of CBR1 has been associated with poor prognosis in uterine endometrial cancer and uterine cervical squamous cell carcinoma. Similarly, decreased CBR1 expression correlates with lymph node metastasis and poor outcomes in ovarian cancer. Conversely, inducing CBR1 expression in ovarian tumors has been shown to result in spontaneous tumor size reduction. Recent research has demonstrated that CBR1 reduces apoptosis and enhances cell survival in pancreatic β-cell lines under conditions of glucotoxicity and glucolipotoxicity by decreasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. In pancreatic islets isolated from db/db mice, a model of type 2 diabetes, both CBR1 expression levels and enzymatic activity were found to be reduced. These findings suggest that CBR1 may protect pancreatic β-cells from oxidative stress under glucotoxic or glucolipotoxic conditions, and its diminished expression or activity may contribute to β-cell dysfunction in type 2 diabetes. Additionally, CBR1 appears to play a pivotal role in the synthesis of prostaglandin F2α (PGF2α) in human amnion fibroblasts. Cortisol has been shown to promote the conversion of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) into PGF2α through glucocorticoid receptor (GR)-mediated induction of CBR1 expression in these fibroblasts. This stimulatory effect of cortisol on CBR1 may partially explain the concurrent increases in cortisol and PGF2α observed in human amnion tissue during labor. These findings may also account for the elevated production of PGF2α in fetal membranes prior to the onset of labor. CBR1 has been shown to interact with cortisol, the C2 domain, and flavonoids.
